newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian police raid arms caches to stop terror.
newsitem.headline: Colombian police raid arms caches to stop terror.

text.p: Anti-narcotics police arrested the suspected No.2 of the Atlantic Coast drug cartel and seized arms caches belonging to the Norte del Valle cartel, a national police official said on Thursday.

The Norte del Valle cartel is said to be fast filling the power vacuum created by last year's capture of the once-mighty kingpins of the Cali drug mafia. The nationwide operation began on Wednesday afternoon and focused on the country's four largest cities and the Caribbean island of San Andres.

It comes against the backdrop of a campaign of bombings and death threats directed at those lawmakers who have publicly backed moves to introduce stiffer penalties for drug crimes and lift Colombia's five-year ban on extradition.

"Everything indicates that this organisation (the Norte del valle cartel) wants to unleash a campaign of narco-terrorism in retaliation for what the government is trying to introduce in terms of stiffer penalties and an end to the ban on extradition," Gen. Luis Enrique Montenegro, deputy chief of the National Police, told reporters in Cali during part of the crackdown, dubbed Operation Cyclone.

He blamed the cartel for a spate of recent bomb attacks in Medellin, the former stronghold of legendary, late drug lord Pablo Escobar, and in the capital of Bogota, where a small device exploded outside government offices last week.

He said the gang probably was also behind a powerful car bomb that police defused last week in Colombia's second largest city, Cali, home to the criminal organisation said to be responsible for 80 percent of the world cocaine supply.

During the two-day offensive, police searched scores of homes in Bogota, Medellin, Cali, Barranquilla and San Andres. In addition to firearms, Montenegro said, police confiscated a $6-million luxury plane.

Part of the squad combing the Caribbean coastal port of Barranquilla on Thursday arrested Guillermo Leon Sanchez, said to be the second-in-command of the Atlantic Coast cartel. Montenegro said the Search Block continued to hunt for chieftains of the Norte del Valle including Oscar Sanchez.

In a recent interview with one of Colombia's top magazines, jailed Cali kingpin Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela said Sanchez was the most feared trafficker in Colombia and had close ties with Mexican narco-baron Amado Carrillo Fuentes.
In the late 1980s and early 1990s, Escobar's Medellin cartel waged a war of bombings, kidnappings and murders to force congress to impose a ban on extradition in 1991.
